READING

**Quantifying the problem**

The numbers Marged has already given validate each other neatly. Eighteen pallets a day, collections every four days, means 72 spaces are needed at peak. She holds 52 pro-rata entitlement. The 20-space gap, sustained over eleven days after the entitlement ran out, produced 18.2 tonnes at the processor. At the £2.48/kg price difference (£3.10 − £0.62) that is exactly £45,136 — the figure she cites. That annual loss is the baseline against which both courses must be measured.

**What each course actually costs**

*TREGOWAN*

| Item | Amount |
|---|---|
| Seasonal rental, 30 spaces | £24,000 |
| Haulage, 14 miles × season | £7,200 |
| **Annual recurring cost** | **£31,200** |

No capital is tied up, but the £31,200 is paid every season indefinitely. The 82 spaces (52 + 30) cover the 72-space requirement with only a 10-space margin, and the 30 rented spaces are 14 miles away from the farm, adding a daily logistics step that the buyer has already noticed.

*HAVERSHOLT*

| Item | Amount | Timing |
|---|---|---|
| Purchase price | £96,000 | Now |
| Additional compressor share (50% less 25%) | £65,000 | Within 3 years |
| **Total incremental capital** | **£161,000** | |

After buying, Marged holds 104 spaces — 32 more than needed, all on site, all seasons, no annual fee. She also holds half the votes on every store decision.

Note on the compressor baseline: Marged already owes 25% × £260,000 = £65,000 regardless of which course she takes. The incremental cost of HAVERSHOLT over the status quo on the compressor is only the additional £65,000, not the full £130,000. The full £130,000 is her share if she buys, versus £65,000 if she does not; the difference is £65,000.

**The payback arithmetic**

TREGOWAN costs £31,200 per year forever (or for as long as Ilsington Chilled will sell the spaces and the buyer will tolerate the handling). HAVERSHOLT's total incremental cash over the status quo is £161,000 spread within three years. Simply dividing: £161,000 ÷ £31,200 = 5.2 years. A fruit farm expected to operate for decades clears that horizon easily. Beyond year five, HAVERSHOLT costs nothing; TREGOWAN keeps running at £31,200 a year.

Looked at another way: the £45,136 annual saving from solving the chilling problem applies equally under both courses. The question is therefore purely how much it costs to deliver those spaces. On-site owned spaces cost £161,000 once; rented off-site spaces cost £31,200 every year.

**Capital adequacy check**

Marged has £140,000. After the £96,000 purchase she holds £44,000. The compressor at 50% is £130,000 due within three years. She is short £86,000 on the compressor if nothing else changes. But the problem is self-funding: the £45,136 per year she stops losing generates roughly £135,000 over three seasons, well exceeding the £86,000 gap even after allowing for farm working capital. She will need to manage cash flow carefully, but the arithmetic closes without external borrowing if she is disciplined. TREGOWAN, by contrast, would leave the compressor share at £65,000 while adding £31,200 every year — a slower drain but one that never ends.

**The pre-emption risk**

Ardwick has 30 days to match Marged's offer. If Ardwick exercises pre-emption, the shares go to Ardwick at £96,000 and Marged remains at 25%. In that scenario HAVERSHOLT simply fails and she must execute TREGOWAN instead, having lost nothing except the time spent. The downside of attempting HAVERSHOLT is therefore bounded: she is not locked out of TREGOWAN by trying first. The booking deadline for TREGOWAN is 2027-03-31, well after the 30-day Ardwick window has closed whichever way it falls.

**Governance value**

At 50% Marged can block any resolution at the store — including the timing and specification of the compressor replacement, future rule changes to the peak entitlement formula, and any future disposal of spaces. At 25% she is a minority shareholder with no veto. Given that the compressor decision is imminent and Ardwick, at 50%, already controls outcomes unilaterally, the governance uplift from 25% to 50% has real practical value: she can insist on competitive tenders, phase the capital expenditure, or negotiate shared financing. With TREGOWAN she has none of that leverage.

**The buyer signal**

The buyer has already raised a query about extra handling. In fresh berry supply, shelf life and chain-of-custody are not marginal concerns; they are the product. TREGOWAN introduces a 14-mile transit, a second loading event, and additional handling time on fruit that is already on the clock. The query may or may not become a formal requirement or a price reduction, but it is a real commercial risk that HAVERSHOLT eliminates entirely.

**Summary of the case**

HAVERSHOLT costs more capital in the short run and carries Ardwick pre-emption risk. TREGOWAN costs less capital but runs at £31,200 per year, introduces supply-chain quality risk that the buyer has flagged, and leaves Marged as a powerless minority shareholder facing a £65,000 compressor bill and no governance say in how or when it lands. The financial crossover is around five years; the strategic and quality crossover is immediate. For a fruit farm with a multi-decade horizon, HAVERSHOLT is the dominant choice.

---

READING
  The decisive comparison is the crossover between HAVERSHOLT's one-time incremental cost of £161,000 and TREGOWAN's perpetual annual cost of £31,200: HAVERSHOLT pays back in roughly five years and then runs at zero recurring cost, while TREGOWAN continues to cost £31,200 every season indefinitely, carries buyer-relationship and quality risk from the off-site handling, and leaves Marged as a minority shareholder with no governance over the compressor replacement that is already approaching. Capital is tight but self-funding: the £45,136 annual saving from solving the chilling problem generates enough cash over three seasons to bridge the compressor shortfall without borrowing. The Ardwick pre-emption risk is real but bounded — if Ardwick matches, Marged loses nothing except time and can fall back to TREGOWAN before its March 2027 booking deadline.

CALL
  HAVERSHOLT

GROUNDS
  HAVERSHOLT's one-time incremental outlay of £161,000 breaks even against TREGOWAN's £31,200 annual recurring cost in roughly five years, after which it costs nothing, while TREGOWAN compounds indefinitely, introduces buyer-queried quality risk from off-site handling, and leaves Marged a powerless minority at the approaching compressor decision.
